blog_summary: The blog post discusses 'Liquid', a new nearline data integration stack developed at LinkedIn to address the limitations of legacy MapReduce/(H)DFS models for handling high-volume append-only data. Adrian Colyer highlights Liquid's ability to support low-latency, incremental processing with resource isolation, contrasting it with traditional batch-oriented systems like MapReduce. The key insight is the need for a unified architecture that bridges online, nearline, and offline processing while avoiding the pitfalls of Lambda and Kappa architectures. Liquid achieves this through a two-layer design: a Kafka-based messaging layer for high-availability storage and rewindability, and a Samza-based processing layer for stateful stream processing with guaranteed service levels. The system's scalability, fault tolerance, and operational robustness are emphasized, along with its real-world use cases at LinkedIn.
paper_title: Liquid: Unifying Nearline and Offline Big Data Integration
paper_abstract: With more sophisticated data-parallel processing systems, the new bottleneck in data-intensive companies shifts from the back-end data systems to the data integration stack, which is responsible for the pre-processing of data for back-end applications. The use of back-end data systems with different access latencies and data integration requirements poses new challenges that current data integration stacks based on distributed file systems—proposed a decade ago for batch-oriented processing—cannot address. In this paper, we describe Liquid, a data integration stack that provides low latency data access to support near real-time in addition to batch applications. It supports incremental processing, and is cost-efficient and highly available. Liquid has two layers: a processing layer based on a stateful stream processing model, and a messaging layer with a highly-available publish/subscribe system. We report our experience of a Liquid deployment with backend data systems at LinkedIn, a data-intensive company with over 300 million users.
